v1.0.1 — a node that fits a home connection, and a join that gets through a busy peer

**Same chain, no coordinated update.** Replace the binary and restart; your data, your key and
your stake stay. Nothing in this release changes consensus, the chain state or the messages nodes
exchange, and nodes on 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 work together. **Every operator should update anyway:** the
first change below takes load off every node on the network, and it does so in proportion to how
many nodes run it.

**Less traffic for everyone**

- **A finished block is published again only by its proposer.** In 1.0.0 every validator that
  finalized a block sent its own copy, each with the precommits it had collected — the copies
  differ in bytes, so the network carried every block once per validator, to every peer (measured
  on 2026-10-13 at fifteen validators: about five copies of every ~100 KB block reached each node).
  The validators that finalized a block do not need it; the nodes that do need one copy.
- **A node outside the validator set** (no stake, pending or jailed — the node beside a desktop
  wallet, an exchange's node, a follower) no longer takes votes, proposals or gossiped copies of
  blocks at all. It follows the chain by block sync, even at the tip, so each block arrives once.
  It hears everything again on the tick its key enters the set. The log says *"Not in the
  validator set — following the chain by block sync …"*.
- **A node far behind and catching up** (more than 1,000 blocks behind the tip its peers announce,
  and its own height rising) stops listening to gossip until it is within 100 blocks, so its line
  is free for the blocks it is fetching. If catching up stalls for 90 seconds it listens again —
  a peer announcing a false tip cannot keep a node deaf.
- **Block-sync requests adapt to the line:** one that times out is followed by a smaller one, and
  every answer that arrives grows the next again.

**Running a validator on a home connection**

Two settings, both off unless you set them:

- `HELIX_P2P_RELAY=off` — this node receives and acts on everything and sends its own votes,
  proposals and blocks, but passes nothing of other nodes on. A relay sends every message it
  receives to every other peer, which on a thin upload is most of what goes out. With relay off a
  validator also follows finished blocks by block sync instead of hearing every peer's copy of them
  (the largest part of the download); it still hears every proposal and vote, so it finalizes each
  block itself, and the block it proposes still reaches everyone. Leave relay on if other nodes
  reach the network only through yours.
- `HELIX_RPC_SYNC_RATE=<rate>`, for example `400K` — paces the block batches other nodes fetch from
  this node's RPC: one at a time, at that rate, only in the compact form. Without it, several
  joining nodes at once share a thin upload so thinly that none of their batches finishes and they
  retry forever. Set it well below the line's upload rate; a tunnel adds its own overhead.

Details: [On a home connection](https://github.com/silvra-net/helix/blob/master/docs/running-a-node.md#on-a-home-connection).

**Joining from a checkpoint**

- A node joining with `HELIX_TRUSTED_CHECKPOINT` fetches the anchor block as one block, and when
  its sync peer answers "busy" it waits and asks again instead of giving the snapshot up and
  replaying the chain from genesis. In 1.0.0 a correct checkpoint could end in a full replay
  through a peer that was only busy.
- Take a fresh checkpoint: `GET /sync/checkpoint` names one a node can actually serve. Ask more
  than one node and compare — the checkpoint is what your node trusts, so it should not come from
  the one node it then syncs from alone.

**Smaller things**

- "Block gap detected" is written at most once a minute and says what fills the gap (it was
  written for every block a lagging node heard — 16,000 times an hour).
- A value of `HELIX_P2P_RELAY` that is not yes/no, and a zero or unreadable `HELIX_RPC_SYNC_RATE`,
  stop the start instead of doing the opposite of what was meant.
